newsitem.title: UK: London futures contract marks new era for Euro gas.
newsitem.headline: London futures contract marks new era for Euro gas.

text.p: The launch of a natural gas futures contract by the International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) on Friday marks the coming of age of the natural gas market in Britain, market participants said on Thursday.
Although the launch has been on hold for months because of technical delays, the industry agrees about the need for the contract and seems optimistic about its chance of success.

"It will be a sad day if it doesn't take off," said Simon Watson, futures broker at FIMAT, which has started a joint operation with broker PVM and will be one of 10 brokers able to execute orders on the contract when trade gets underway at 1000 GMT on Friday.
"I hope it all works, not least for all at the IPE. They have put in an immense amount of effort," he said.
Consumer pressure for clean energy, new gas-fired power technology and European Union deregulation combine to make natural gas Europe's fuel of choice for the next century.

An unregulated "over the counter" (OTC) spot market in natural gas has been in existence in London for a couple of years once sellers other than the once state monopoly British Gas Plc were gradually allowed to supply industrial consumers.
From April 1996, sellers have also been able to supply some households with gas ahead of the liberalisation of the entire residential market in 1998.

Spot market players say they are ready to use more sophisticated instruments like the IPE contract to allow them to hedge their price exposure. The markets will also result in greater price transparency, they said.
"I reckon there's a potential for 20 companies to be there on Day One", said FIMAT's Watson.

However, not all participants may be ready to go from the start because of time-consuming paperwork involved in opening an account and registering with the Securities and Futures Authority (SFA), Watson said.
"Three trading houses have done everything necessary and will have trading screens in their own offices," he said. "The others will be relying on phoning brokers to put their orders in."
Watson believes that if the contract succeeds, the number of market players could rise to 40 within two months.
Louise Kitchen, director of gas trading at Enron Capital and Trade Resources Ltd, said that gas giant Enron is planning to use the contract.
"Enron will be placing orders on the initial day," she said.

She believes that the main benefits of the contract will be transparency in pricing; an increase in market liquidity; and an increase in the number of participants as the market attracts companies such as financial houses not trading gas now.
"It's been a long time in coming. It's here finally so let's give it all we can. The market needs it to encourage new players," Kitchen added.
"For the first time the market truly offers the possibility of a hedging option which is useful," one gas trader said.
This trader also said the IPE market would also reduced credit risk since all trades must go through the London Clearing House.
Some players feel traders may be drawn to the IPE contract because it offers the possibility of physical delivery, and futures brokers are charging less than OTC brokers.
"I've heard that," said Bryan Hunt, OTC broker with EES.
But he believes brokers may be forced to raise their fees if business is slow.

"If the volume doesn't happen, they (futures brokers) will have to raise their fees as it won't be economical," he said, adding: "to engage in a commission war before the game's even started is stupid."
